Putrefy

PYOO-truh-fy · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To putrefy is to decay or rot and produce a foul smell.

Without refrigeration, the meat left on the counter started to putrefy within hours.

Worked Example

The biology teacher warned the class that the dissected specimen would putrefy quickly once removed from its preservative jar.

Putrefy is a fairly clinical, scientific word for the specific biological process of organic matter rotting and giving off a foul odor.

Your Turn

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

rot: Rot is the everyday word for decay -- food rots, wood rots, and nobody reaches for a dictionary. Putrefy names the same process in precise, almost scientific language, and it points squarely at the foul smell of flesh or food breaking down. Kitchens say rot; lab reports say putrefy.

decompose: To decompose is to break down into simpler parts through natural decay -- grass clippings decompose quietly in a compost bin, and scientists use it as a neutral, technical term. To putrefy is narrower and fouler: rotting that gives off a terrible smell. Everything that putrefies is decomposing, but much decomposes without any stench.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

preserve: keep from decaying

cure: treat to prevent spoiling

Where it sits · how far the decay has gone — spoil → putrefy → liquefy

spoil vs. putrefy: Food can spoil and merely turn -- milk gone sour, bread gone stale -- an early stage of decay far milder than putrefying, which is rotting all the way through with a foul smell.

liquefy vs. putrefy: Something so far gone it liquefies has decayed even further than simply putrefying.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — putr

Root — putr: rotten (from Latin putris, 'rotten')

Suffix — -efy

Suffix — -efy: to make, to cause to become (Latin -ficare; spelled -efy in a handful of English verbs like liquefy and stupefy)

Put it together

Put it together: putr ("rotten," from Latin putris) + -efy ("to make," the same ending as in liquefy) = to make rotten -- to decay.

Use the root in a new word: putrid

Use the root in a new word: putrid: The same root gives us "putrid," the everyday adjective for something that smells rotten.
